text: A vector isn't an arrow — it's a list of numbers that obeys a fixed set of rules, and every quantum algorithm you'll study later is, underneath the physics vocabulary, just linear algebra operating on vectors like these.

A set V is a vector space if, for any vectors u, v, w and scalars a and b, five things hold: closure, so u plus v and a times u both stay inside V; commutativity and associativity of addition; a zero vector, with v plus zero equal to v; and scalar distributivity, so a times the quantity u plus v equals a u plus a v. No arrows, no angles — just algebra, which is exactly why the same toolkit works for real columns, complex columns, or quantum states.

Addition and scalar multiplication in R squared work coordinate by coordinate. Adding 2,3 and 4, negative 1 gives 6,2 — add matching coordinates. Multiplying 2,3 by the scalar 3 gives 6,9 — scale every coordinate. Both results checked by direct calculation, nothing approximate.

A qubit's state lives in C squared, the space of ordered pairs of complex numbers. The two pure computational states, ket-zero and ket-one, are 1,0 and 0,1 — structurally identical to R squared's standard basis vectors. The only difference is the entries are allowed to be complex, which is exactly what lets a qubit represent a superposition state. Every rule you learn for real vector spaces carries over to C squared without changing a word.
Next lesson tackles which sets of vectors actually qualify as a valid set of reference directions — span, basis, and a hands-on determinant test for linear independence.
